name: Pentoxifylline topical

lead: Pentoxifylline is a xanthine-derived vasodilator that improves blood flow and reduces inflammation. Taken by mouth it is approved for leg pain from poor circulation; in appearance contexts, creams and gels containing it have been explored for cellulite and skin dimpling.

The proposed route to a smoother look is better microcirculation in skin and underlying tissue. Published work consists of reviews, a dermatology overview and pilot-scale reports rather than large trials.

paras: In cosmetic discussions it is a topical cream or gel applied to affected areas. Compounded or cosmetic products vary, and use is generally off-label.

Oral pentoxifylline commonly causes stomach upset, dizziness and flushing, and can affect bleeding risk. It is prescription-only in the US, UK, Canada and Australia. Topical use is described as better tolerated, with limited data.

chain: Improved local blood flow and reduced inflammation
angle.text: Cream or gel formulations are discussed for cellulite, with the idea that improved microcirculation reduces dimpling. Evidence for this use is limited to small reports.

lead: Pentoxifylline, also called oxpentifylline, is a prescription drug in the xanthine family. Its only labelled use is relieving leg symptoms from intermittent claudication in peripheral artery disease.[1] It acts as a non-selective phosphodiesterase inhibitor, lowers TNF and leukotriene synthesis, improves red-cell flexibility and reduces blood viscosity.[1]

In appearance contexts, topical or transdermal formulations have been described for cellulite, with the aim of improving dermal microcirculation and reducing dimpling.[2][1] A 2023 review in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology surveys its dermatology uses.[3]
Dermatologists use it in other skin contexts, such as treatment of vasculitis and wound healing reviews, though most trials concern oral use for unrelated conditions.

paras: Oral pentoxifylline is approved for intermittent claudication; off-label uses include venous leg ulcers, diabetic neuropathy, sarcoidosis, alcoholic hepatitis and several others.[1] Transdermal use for cellulite is noted in encyclopedic coverage.[1]
It raises intracellular cAMP by inhibiting phosphodiesterases, reduces inflammatory mediators, improves blood flow properties and lowers platelet aggregation.[1]

Common effects of the oral drug include belching, bloating, nausea, dizziness and flushing; rarer ones include palpitations, allergic reactions and bleeding. It is contraindicated with recent retinal or cerebral haemorrhage or bleeding risk.[1]

A 2023 review, Pentoxifylline in dermatology, summarises dermatologic applications.[3] Trials listed for pentoxifylline mostly involve oral treatment of conditions such as alcoholic hepatitis, type 2 diabetes complications and muscular dystrophy.[4] Limited pilot trials and case series on topical cellulite use are described in secondary sources.[2]
